ADDED i3: --- Alphabets used as building blocks for the converters under test. ---
ADDED i4: The space character plus the 26 lower-case English letters.
ADDED i5: Digits, both letter cases of the English alphabet, and a space.
ADDED i6: Digits, the lower-case English alphabet, and a space.
ADDED i7: The ten decimal digits.
ADDED i8: A two-symbol alphabet, useful for forcing multi-character encodings.
ADDED i9: A Hebrew alphabet (preceded by underscore and space separators). Expressed as Unicode code points (U+05D0 .. U+05EA are the Hebrew letters) so the exact charact
ADDED i10: Original alphabet expressed as code points, mixing BMP and supplementary characters.
ADDED i11: Lower-case English alphabet expressed as code points (space followed by a-z).
ADDED i13: Builds a string from the given Unicode code points. Used to spell out non-Latin sample text unambiguously, without relying on the source file's character encodi
ADDED i14: Builds the converter from the class Javadoc's "Sample usage" example: original {@code a, b, c, d} encoded with {@code 0, 1, d} while leaving {@code d} unencoded

ADDED i15: Verifies the full contract of a converter built from the given alphabets:
  • it can be serialized to a map and reconstructed into an equal converter,
ADDED i16: A converter reconstructed from its serialized map must be indistinguishable from the original.
ADDED i19: Decoding the encoded form must reproduce the input exactly.
ADDED i20: Binary encoded as digits, digits encoded as binary, and letters encoded as binary.
ADDED i21: A single distinct character '+' used as the original, encoding and do-not-encode alphabet.
ADDED i22: A converter is never equal to a bare Character.
ADDED i23: With a single distinct original character, each character maps to one encoded character.
ADDED i24: A null encoding alphabet cannot be used to build a converter.
ADDED i25: Mutating the source map after the first converter is built yields a different converter.
ADDED i26: Decoding null is a no-op that returns null; the converter remains a single-char-length converter.
ADDED i27: Lower-case letters are left unencoded, so only the upper-case portions are converted.
ADDED i28: Digits are left unencoded instead.
ADDED i29: '3' is not part of the BINARY original alphabet, so it cannot be encoded.
ADDED i30: Converter built from a single 'R' character...
ADDED i31: ...is not equal to a converter built from an empty map.
ADDED i32: A converter built from an empty alphabet is never equal to null.
ADDED i33: A converter is always equal to itself (reflexivity).
ADDED i34: Hebrew round-trips through both a binary and a numeric encoding alphabet, and vice versa.
ADDED i36: '0' is in the do-not-encode list but absent from the (lower-case) encoding alphabet.
ADDED i37: '0' is in the do-not-encode list but absent from the (lower-case) original alphabet.
ADDED i38: Every encoding character is also in the do-not-encode list, leaving zero usable encoding characters.
ADDED i39: The encoding alphabet is the digits plus '_'; all digits are do-not-encode, leaving only '_'.
ADDED i40: The trailing '0' is an incomplete encoded group (each group is two characters long).
ADDED i41: "XX" is not a known encoded group for the Javadoc-example converter.
